facts.claim: Tribal Leadership (2008) is by Dave Logan, John King and Halee Fischer-Wright; the TR edition title is Kabile Liderliği. Main authors Logan, King, Fischer-Wright, so 'Dave Logan' alone as sole author is incomplete.
The authors describe a study of more than 24,000 people in about two dozen companies; Gallup's write-up calls it a ten-year study (another source says more than eight years).
facts.source: Gallup Business Journal; Chief Learning Officer

facts.claim: Tribes are natural groups of roughly 20 to 150 people that form regardless of the org chart.
Five stages, each with its own language: 1 'Life sucks', 2 'My life sucks', 3 'I'm great (and you're not)', 4 'We're great', 5 'Life is great'.

Listed shares of the organizations/people studied: stage 1 about 2%, stage 2 about 25%, stage 3 about 49%, stage 4 about 22%, stage 5 about 2%. Scope of the denominator is not stated in the secondary source.

Stage 3: people compete for personal wins, hoard knowledge, relate in two-person pairs; the most common words are 'I', then 'me' and 'my'. Stage three people complain they are too busy and have no time and poor support.
Tribal leadership focuses on two things: the words people use and the types of relationships they form.
Leverage rule: speak at most one stage above where the group is.

Stage 3 to 4 leverage: ask open-ended questions to learn what people value, then build projects too big to finish without partnering; encourage three-person relationships (triads) anchored on shared values.

Stage 4: members share values and knowledge; competition shifts outward to another tribe or company; the rule 'the bigger the foe, the more powerful the tribe'; relationships are triads built on shared values.
Stage 5: 'innocent wonderment', 'life is great'; about 2% of the time and unstable; the team that built the first Macintosh is the cited example; such teams often drop back to stage 4 to regroup.
Stage-four leaders suggest regular 'oil changes': team conversations about what is working, what is not, and how to fix it.
Gallup piece reports some stage-four groups claimed 'a three thousand percent increase in profitability' over stage three.

rejected.claim: Logan alone studied 24,000 employees 'over ten years' (old text)
rejected.reason: Three authors; duration varies by source. Use 'the authors' and 'more than 24,000 people in about two dozen companies'.

rejected.claim: Stage-5 groups 'made history performances' / stage 4 trap is a common enemy with a Logan quote 'identity built around a common enemy dissolves when the enemy vanishes'
rejected.reason: Quote not found. The book's stage-four adversary rule is supported; the quote is not.

rejected.claim: Apple's 'fight IBM' identity changed over time
rejected.reason: Not confirmed from the sources found. Apple appears only as a stage-five example in the Gallup text; Macintosh team via fs.blog.

rejected.claim: 'Tribal leader does not give directives' quote; leaders as 'node points' bridging groups; mediating tension at a meeting by pointing to a shared customer-experience value
rejected.reason: Quote and scene not found; the supported point is the words/relationships focus and the triad move.

rejected.claim: Fifth-stage tribes spread leadership to everyone

1498.note: Five stages as a listening tool; stage-three words I/me/my; leader listens to the words.

1499.note: Stage four runs on a foe; macintosh team as stage five; quote and Apple-IBM claim dropped.
